questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I love to travel and have always wanted to go to Australia so what better opportunity than exchange? I actually thought I would prefer being on the east coast but I am so happy that I got to go to Western Australia even though it was not my first priority. I really think that this part of Australia is so underrated and has so much to offer and explore which for me was very important.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: UWA was really good at passing on information and it was easy to navigate the website to find what you needed. If by chance you could not find it every member of the study abroad team was super helpful and fast at replying.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There were an orientation week for all the exchange students before uni strat. Here we got a ton of important information like how to navigate campus, use lms (the same as canvas), where to find information and got to ask questions if we had any. There were arranged some "team building"-"get to know each other"- activities during the day time which were nice but not really anything to expand our social life after school-hours (unless you were a collage resident).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Overall orientation was good but I would have loved if they had arranged some evening/night activities as well.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I did not find any housing before arriving as previous travel reports suggested that you should just find something once in Perth. However, this semester was the first one back after Covid-19 which resulted in a major "housing crisis". It was tough to find accommodation so when I got offered a room I just accepted it. I ended up living at the Switch in the CBD which was a bit expensive but had some great facilities. However, I would have preferred to live in a shared house or at one of the colleges, so I would recommend either applying to the colleges or seeing if you can find some housing before arrival and then maybe keep on looking on flatmates, facebook e.t.c to see if you can find something cheaper or better

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The university does not really arrange any social activities so when you are living off campus you should be prepared to arrange them yourself. If you are living at the colleges on campus there are a ton of social life, parties and activities (maybe more like the student life we know in Denmark) so it would be easier to get a social life however it might also be a bit of a commitment as you properly don't have much time for people/life outside of the college. If you live off or on campus in Perth I would recommend buying a car! Public transport in Western Australia is not that great and everything is a bit far away so it is kind of necessary to have a car if you want to explore as much as possible. I shared a car with 2 other girls and we bought it very cheap (AU$2700) of Facebook marketplace and it was a great investment. Just have in mind that it can be hard to get a parking permit in Perth, so it is by far easier if you live on campus or a place with parking included. Also have in mind that there will be some expenses when owning a car like registration, gas, insurance etc. however I really believe it was worth it especially because we were able to sell it for a bit more than we bought it for and then you do not need to rent a car while on exchange of for travelling after.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I think the registration process was a bit difficult in some areas but the study abroad team were so helpful and so fast at replying to mails!

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I can't really remember it in detail to be honest but it was just to follow the steps online and fill in the appropriate information. And if you had any questions it was easy to contact the study abroad team and get help.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The study abroad team <3 I send them a ton of mails with every little problem/question and they never failed to help me or fix the problems for me.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was very successful with registering for classes. I got all of my first priorities except the ones that I was not eligible for. As a bachelor student, you are not allowed to enrol in any master unit and as an exchange student from KU, you are not allowed to take any units at the school of medicine which is nice to know when looking at units.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Look at the timetable for the units when choosing what you want to choose. This can help you avoid too many schedule clashes and is also a great way to choose units that will give you a desirable schedule so you can avoid mandatory classes Friday afternoon if you are planning a weekend trip somewhere (just nice to have in mind).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I choose 3 first-year units and only 1 third-year unit so as a third-year student the level was lower than back home.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: All the lectures were recorded and uploaded so you do not really have to show up in person at any point if you do not want to. However, most of the units have tutorials which are either mandatory or your participation will be a part of your assessment and count in your final grade. Throughout the semester you will have tests, assignments etc. which are a part of your assessment too so it is a bit important to be aware of this. For most units, you will have been through around 50% of your assessment before the final exam which means that the exam only counts 50% of your final score. So if you do well during the semester you can be lucky to pass the units before the exam or only have to score a small amount of points on the exam which is nice when you have multiple to study for.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Neuroscience in society (NEUR1001), Advanced Neuroscience 1 (NEUR3301), Drugs that changed the world (PHAR1101), Active leadership 1: Developing leadership skills (SSEH1104)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Active leadership 1: Developing leadership skills. This is not a unit where you get academically challenged (at all) but this is a great unit to actually get some friends in school and have fun with other exchange students as well as the locals. It is more like a "sports science unit" based on teamwork and leadership techniques challenged in group dynamics during task solving on a mountain bike, a paddleboard or in a kayak.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I bought a car which of course give some unexpected costs like insurance, registration, mechanic bills and gas,

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The price of vegetables is really depending on the season. A cucumber costed 20dkk the first months but ended up being more like 5-10dkk at the end of the semester. Everything organic was crazy expensive as well and some of the fruits like grapes were just expensive all the time (75-100 dkk/pr kg).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was really satisfied with the work that UWA sport did for the exchange students. They had arranged 6 weeks of programs for the exchange students to join different sports. I joined the squash program which was really nice (a bit slow in the beginning but it got better). In terms of other non-academic opportunities, I was not too satisfied. There was one "join a non-academic club"-fair but most of the clubs did not even have a stand so In my opinion it was not the best. However, I did not really do anything myself to become a part of any of the clubs so that might also play a role.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
At UWA sport it was possible to play tennis, squash, and volleyball, do stand-up paddleball or join the gym. At the gym you could also do yoga-, zumba-, cross-fit- and other classes. There was also an outdoor pool at the university which you could be a member card to and use in the opening hours. 
One time the school's Electronic Music Appreciation Club arranged a festival/concert/party-thing called eclipse which was pretty fun. We found the event on Facebook so maybe there would have been more things like that if we knew where to look but I am not sure.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Find a friend and take them to some of the UWA sports activities. It is kind of nice to have something to do together with some of the other exchange students as well even though it is not so, thing crazy. You can also join some of the gym classes or just rent out a squash court every now and then. I also met a girl who signed up for a ceramic class every Wednesday (not anything connected to UWA tho) which sounded really fun.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Buy a car/rent a car and drive as far up and down as you can. I really enjoyed the coastal way and towns up til Exmouth (north) and down south around Albany and Denmark. The nature is so beautiful and diverse in Western Australia, it is amazing! I have been told that Karijini National Park should be incredible but I did not have the time to go there as it is far from Perth.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: All the Australians are so nice so it was pretty easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: From my experience, most of the local students don't really go to school to find friends. A lot of them have friends from high school, work etc. and when you don't follow all the same units it can be hard to really connect. They are all very friendly but it is easier to connect with the other exchange students. If you want some local friends I would recommend finding a job or renting a room in a shared house where you can have Australian roomies.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing I can think of.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I really appreciated how nice the Australians are. Everyone is super helpful and I especially member when I was travelling in the mid-semester break when two guys offered to help us get some air out of our tiers so we could go to this really nice snorkel spot and also showed us the way there.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Bring some warm clothes and a rain jacket! Even though it is Australia and Perth you arrive in winter which means a lot of rain and cold weather.
2. It is really great to have a car in Western Australia so check out Facebook marketplace and find a good deal.
3. If you think you are gonna struggle financially it is pretty fun to get a job (depending on what of course). You will get to meet some fun local people who can show you the best places in Perth AND the service jobs plays pretty well so it is a win/win. 
(The others were a lot of practical things so I will add one more: 4. Say yes! This is a time when you get the opportunity to experience so many incredible things and sometimes it is important to get out of your comfort zone and go on a road trip with some of your new friends or join a fun club. Even if it seems a bit hard and scary it will be worth it in the end.)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No, I think I covered most of it

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of this experience was the friendships and memories I made. I have had so many incredible moments that I will never forget and it was really rewarding to get out of my comfort zone and just take the experience a day at a time.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I think the greatest challenge was that it was nothing like I thought. It is important to acknowledge that the exchange-experience is really hard to imagine before you are living it. It might not be as you expected but for me, it ended up being even more and giving me a greater outcome than the semester I had expected.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
